articles.title: Read, return, forget: processing passport scans without storing the image
articles.excerpt: Originally published at Read, return, forget: processing passport scans without storing the image A passport photo is the most sensitive file most apps ever receive. It carries a face, a full name, a…
articles.body: Originally published at Read, return, forget: processing passport scans without storing the image A passport photo is the most sensitive file most apps ever receive. It carries a face, a full name, a date of birth and a document number, and it is enough to open an account somewhere else. Yet in many upload flows the picture is copied five or six times before anyone asks whether it needs to exist at all. This post looks at the question from the engineering side: what the GDPR says about keeping data, the places where a passport image quietly piles up, and a pattern called read, return, forget – the image is read, the result is returned, and nothing of the picture is kept.

articles.title: Stop Hand-Rolling JSON Lines With WriteLine. .NET 11 Writes Them for You
articles.excerpt: TL;DR: JsonSerializer.SerializeAsyncEnumerable(stream, items, topLevelValues: true) writes canonical JSON Lines: one compact value per line, LF after every one. No more WriteLine(JsonSerializer.Serial…
articles.body: TL;DR: JsonSerializer.SerializeAsyncEnumerable(stream, items, topLevelValues: true) writes canonical JSON Lines: one compact value per line, LF after every one. No more WriteLine(JsonSerializer.Serialize(x)) loops. This ships in .NET 11, which is at Release Candidate 2 with a go-live license, but is not GA yet. Everything below was run on the .NET 11 RC 1 SDK. The loop everybody has written JSON Lines (JSONL) is one JSON value per line. It is the format of choice for log files, data exports, and anything you want to append to without rewriting the whole file. System.Text.Json could already read it. On .NET 10, DeserializeAsyncEnumerable(stream, topLevelValues: true) streams top-level values just fine.

articles.title: A small metadata contract for reviewing photo crops
articles.excerpt: A photo handoff often includes a final image, an intended destination and a sentence such as “make it square.” That is not quite enough information for another person to review the export. A square fi…
articles.body: A photo handoff often includes a final image, an intended destination and a sentence such as “make it square.” That is not quite enough information for another person to review the export. A square file may be too small for the destination; a large file may have the wrong aspect ratio. Both checks are useful, but they answer different questions. This article builds a tiny, local metadata check for that handoff. It does not open images, alter pixels, inspect content or decide whether an edit is visually good. The code is an independent example, not an integration with any photo service. I am associated with Y2K Photo Lab, and AI assistance helped prepare this article. The examples are hypothetical rather than measurements of real photographs.

articles.title: Password Reset Email Spam: 3 Evidence Boundaries for Seller Recovery
articles.excerpt: An order notification is time-sensitive, but a marketplace cannot treat a seller's password reset as delivered merely because an outbound mail server accepted it. Short answer: password reset emails c…
articles.body: An order notification is time-sensitive, but a marketplace cannot treat a seller's password reset as delivered merely because an outbound mail server accepted it. Short answer: password reset emails can land in spam because sender authentication fails or does not align, because the sending domain or infrastructure has a poor reputation, or because recipient filtering considers the message unwanted or suspicious. Authentication helps establish who sent the message; it does not guarantee inbox placement. For a B2B SaaS marketplace, the practical resolution is to preserve evidence at three boundaries: the recovery request, the mail handoff, and the recipient-side observation. Keep them separate.

articles.title: Meet *sshole, the vulnerability that lets hackers SSH into Linux devices
articles.excerpt: Certain configurations of Alpine are affected. Other distros may be as well.
articles.body: Devices running some configurations of Alpine Linux, and possibly other distributions, are affected by a decade-old vulnerability that allows attackers to log into devices with no password. The vulnerability exists in the interaction between OpenSSH, the code library implementing SSH connections, and musl, a lightweight alternative to the libc library that, unlike most other Linux distributions, is used in Alpine. Further, OpenSSH using musl (pronounced muscle) must not use PAM (pluggable authentication modules), a framework that handles user authentication and account-access checks. Alpine is a lightweight, widely used Linux distribution. Other platforms may be affected if they use the same configurations.

articles.title: Blue Origin announces 3rd stage for its powerful New Glenn rocket —and a new engine
articles.excerpt: Blue Origin has developed a third stage for its New Glenn rocket, which it says will make the launcher even more flexible and capable. The company has also built a new engine, called Northstar.
articles.body: Blue Origin's big rocket is getting a little bigger. Jeff Bezos' company announced today (Nov. 5) that it has developed a third stage for its New Glenn rocket, which it says will make the powerful launcher more capable and flexible. The stage, called the GS3, "enhances New Glenn's capabilities," Blue Origin said in a blog post today . "The third stage enables direct deployment of satellite constellations to GEO [ geostationary orbit ] and supports heavy-lift science and exploration missions to the moon and deep space." Illustration of the variants of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, with the new GS3 third stage now in the mix. (Image credit: Blue Origin) New Glenn is a two-stage vehicle at the moment.

articles.title: Earth has captured a new mini moon  — but it won't stick around for long
articles.excerpt: Earth has caught itself a new mini-moon, and QQ8 is sticking around for Christmas.
articles.body: Earth has caught itself a new mini-moon, and it is sticking around for Christmas. The space rock, designated 2026 QQ8, was first observed in August 2026 after entering orbit around Earth in April 2026. The discovery was reported by the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center on Thursday (Oct. 29). The stay of QQ8 is a temporary one. The mini-moon will remain in the thrall of Earth's gravity through December before breaking away in 2027. Scientists have recreated the orbital path of QQ8, finding that it takes 359 days, or about 0.98 of an Earth year, to orbit the sun . QQ8 closely approaches Earth around once every ten years, but this time the object came so close that Earth has been able to gravitationally seize it.
